design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (metafor package in R) of placebo-controlled randomized trials of prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation (OIC): the peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists methylnaltrexone, naloxone (including fixed oxycodone/naloxone), naloxegol, alvimopan, naldemedine and axelopran, and the prescription laxatives lubiprostone and prucalopride. Outcome: relative risk (RR) of failing to respond by each trial's definition, with numbers needed to treat and to harm; GRADE by drug. 27 trials from 26 publications after one outlier was removed; 5390 participants on a drug and 3491 on placebo. An update of Ford et al. (2013). Read as the accepted manuscript (45 PDF pages without printed page numbers), not the published version: pages are cited as PDF pages of the accepted manuscript.
can_establish: The average effect, against placebo, of prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation on the chance of not meeting a trial's response criterion, overall and by drug, in randomized trials up to March 2017 of people taking opioids, mostly for chronic non-cancer pain, together with the excess of common gut side effects and of stopping for side effects.
cannot_establish: Effects in people who use heroin or other non-prescribed opioids or who are on methadone or buprenorphine treatment (the only trial in methadone maintenance was removed as an outlier, and no other included trial is described as in such people); which drug works best (no head-to-head trials); effects of over-the-counter laxatives (not included); benefit or harm beyond 12 weeks; or whether pain control is kept (pain was not an outcome).

sample.recruitment: Literature search by a medical librarian, confirmed by two investigators: MEDLINE (1950-), EMBASE (1975-) and EMBASE Classic (1947-), Web of Science (1900-) and CENTRAL (1996-), all to March 2017, plus bibliographies of highly relevant papers chosen with subject experts (PDF pp. 6-8). Trial participants (Table 1, PDF pp. 26-29): adults taking opioids for chronic non-cancer pain in most trials; advanced illness or cancer pain in four (Bull 2015, Murata 2016, Slatkin 2009, Thomas 2008); after orthopaedic surgery in one (Anissian 2012); one alvimopan trial (Paulson 2005) enrolled people with chronic non-malignant pain or opioid dependence.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Randomized trials of medical therapy for OIC, defined either as constipation associated with starting opioids or as fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements a week with symptoms after starting opioids; any dose; open-label extension periods excluded; trials of organic or chronic idiopathic constipation excluded (PDF pp. 6-7). Of 35 full texts, 9 were excluded, 4 as not placebo-controlled and 5 for data that could not be extracted (Figure 1, PDF p. 36). One small methylnaltrexone trial in a methadone-maintenance programme (Yuan 2000; all 11 on drug and none of 11 on placebo responded) was removed as an outlier (PDF p. 11; Table 1, PDF p. 28).
sample.demographics: Trial sizes from 9 to 803; women 38% to 68% where reported; baseline opioid doses 20 to 2000 mg morphine equivalent where reported (Table 1; PDF p. 19). Several included trials are known only from conference abstracts (Murata 2016; Hale 2016, two trials; Vickery 2014), and one (Spierings 2015) has no journal citation (references, PDF pp. 23-24).
sample.attrition: Data extracted as intention-to-treat, dropouts counted as failures where reporting allowed (PDF p. 9). Dropout for adverse events, in the 20 trials reporting it: 7.4% on drug against 4.7% on placebo (PDF p. 17).
sample.selection_effects: Trials enrolled people with chronic pain who had constipation on stable opioids; people with substance use disorders are not described, and the one trial in people on methadone maintenance was excluded after the funnel plot was inspected. Several trials are known only from abstracts. English-language studies only were found, without a stated language limit.

exposure.measurement: Random allocation to a study drug or placebo within each trial; arms of the same drug at different doses were combined (PDF p. 9).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 1): methylnaltrexone subcutaneous or oral, from a single dose (Slatkin 2009) or 4-7 days (Anissian 2012) to 4 weeks with optional use to 12 weeks; naloxone oral, alone or as prolonged-release oxycodone/naloxone, 3-12 weeks; naloxegol, alvimopan, naldemedine, axelopran, lubiprostone and prucalopride oral, 2-12 weeks. Background opioids varied (oxycodone, morphine, methadone and others) at 20 to 2000 mg morphine equivalent a day where reported (PDF p. 19).
exposure.polysubstance: Not described: other drug use by participants is not reported. Laxative use differed between trials (laxative-refractory status, where reported, was analysed as a moderator).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; participants continued their opioids.

comparison.controls: Placebo within each trial (Table 2 heads the comparisons 'Placebo/Usual Care').
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; trials pooled with random-effects weights.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparisons. Between trials, opioid dose, cancer versus non-cancer pain, laxative history, outcome definition and duration differed and were explored as moderators.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Placebo groups continued the same background opioids.

outcomes.instruments: Each trial's own response definition, most often three or more complete spontaneous bowel movements a week; others include a bowel movement within 4 or 24 hours of a dose, satisfaction with relief, change in quality of life, or no need for laxatives (Table 1; PDF p. 8). Adverse events: any new-onset event, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, nausea and/or vomiting, and dropout for adverse events.
outcomes.validity_norms: No common definition of response; six trials with a stricter definition did not give a different result (PDF p. 13). Trial risk of bias with the Cochrane tool by two reviewers (Supplementary table 2, PDF pp. 40-41), and GRADE by drug (Table 2).
outcomes.operationalization: Failure to respond means not meeting the trial's response criterion. The NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute difference in response. The Methods define the NNH for an adverse event leading to withdrawal (PDF p. 10), but the Results give an NNH for any adverse event (about 21) and a separate one for dropout because of adverse events (36).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six pooled outcomes (failure to respond; any adverse event; diarrhoea; abdominal pain; nausea and/or vomiting; dropout for adverse events), each also by drug or subgroup.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Within trials, mostly double-blind (Supplementary table 2), but that table's yes/no coding has no key.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects RR of failure to respond, drug against placebo: all drugs 0.70 (95% CI 0.64-0.75), 27 trials, Q(26) = 105.0, I2 77.9%, NNT 5; FDA-approved drugs and doses 0.69 (0.62-0.77), NNT 5 (4-7). Response in 2784 of 5390 on drug (printed 51.3%; 51.7% by editors' calculation) against 1157 of 3491 on placebo (33.1%). By drug (Table 2 and text): methylnaltrexone 0.62 (0.49-0.78; forest plot 0.50-0.76), cancer-related pain 0.51 (0.41-0.63), non-cancer 0.75 (0.63-0.90); naloxone 0.63 (0.56-0.71), I2 0%; alvimopan 0.68 (0.58-0.80); naldemedine 0.65 (0.52-0.82); naloxegol 0.77 (0.61-0.97); lubiprostone 0.90 (0.83-0.97), I2 0%; prucalopride, one trial, 0.88 in the text and Table 2 but 0.82 in the forest plot (0.68-0.98); axelopran, one trial, 0.60 (0.44-0.81). NNTs: lubiprostone 15 (9-51), naloxegol 7 (4-26), methylnaltrexone 3.4 (3-6), naloxone 4 (4-6), naldemedine 5 (4-8). Adverse events, 23 trials: any 58.2% against 53.0%, RR 1.10 (1.05-1.16), NNH 20.6 (14.3-36.8); diarrhoea 8.5% against 4.7%; abdominal pain 12.8% against 5.5%; nausea and/or vomiting 11.5% against 10.1%; dropout for adverse events 7.4% against 4.7%, NNH 36 (22-96).
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression: baseline opioid dose predicted the effect (Q(1) = 4.75, p = .029; larger effect at higher doses); placebo response rate did not (p = .145). Subgroups: laxative-refractory populations RR 0.57 (0.47-0.69) against 0.75 (0.69-0.82), p = .009; trials of two weeks or less 0.67 (0.61-0.74) against 0.85 (0.82-0.88) for the other 22, p < 0.001; stricter outcome definition 0.75 against 0.68, p = .364; low-risk-of-bias trials 0.67 (0.58-0.78) against the rest 0.71 (0.64-0.78), p = .63; for methylnaltrexone, cancer-related against non-cancer pain, p = .006.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration number is given; the PRISMA checklist's protocol item points to the Methods, and its search item reads 'Appendix S1 (need to include)' (PDF p. 42).
analysis.selective_reporting: Each trial's pre-specified outcome was used where possible, otherwise another clinically meaningful outcome (PDF p. 8). The outlier trial was removed after inspection of the funnel plot. Absolute risks per drug appear in Table 2 but not in the abstract.
analysis.power: Not applicable; 27 trials, 8881 participants. Prucalopride and axelopran rest on one trial each.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 27 placebo-controlled trials in people taking opioids mostly for chronic pain, prescription medicines for OIC raised the share meeting the trial's response criterion from about 33 to about 52 in 100, with marked heterogeneity between trials and drugs and an asymmetric funnel plot; diarrhoea and abdominal pain were more common on the drugs, and slightly more people stopped because of side effects.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the opioid-receptor blockers are 'safe and effective' (PDF p. 5). The Discussion says all studies showed superiority over placebo and that the analysis confirms their safety 'while maintaining opioid analgesic affect' (PDF p. 18). The forest plot (PDF p. 38) shows four trials whose intervals include no effect (Irving 2011, Jamal 2015, Spierings, Liu 2002); pain was not an outcome of the review; safety rests on trials of 12 weeks or less with an excess of side effects. The abstract says study duration did not affect the result, while the Results report a significantly larger effect in trials of two weeks or less (PDF p. 13). Funnel-plot asymmetry was significant even after the outlier was removed (PDF p. 11) but did not enter the GRADE ratings.

timeline.event: Ford, Brenner and Schoenfeld, meta-analysis of 17 trials concluding that the opioid-receptor blockers are safe and effective for OIC (as described on PDF p. 6); this review updates it and shares most of its trials (Table 1 marks the newer ones).
This review: 27 trials, adding naloxegol and naldemedine.

replication.where_it_stands: An update of Ford et al. (2013) with the same conclusion; the two share most trials and are not independent confirmations. Trials published after March 2017 are not included, and no included trial tested over-the-counter laxatives or enrolled people who use non-prescribed opioids.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no relevant conflicts of interest (PDF p. 3).
funding.affiliations_note: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Boston), Bedford Veterans Administration Medical Center and the University of Florida.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials in people who use heroin or other non-prescribed opioids and in people on methadone or buprenorphine treatment, comparing these medicines with each other and with over-the-counter laxatives, with pain, withdrawal symptoms and side effects measured over months.

Five databases with dates, a librarian, bibliographies and subject experts; strategies are printed (PDF p. 39) but omit methylnaltrexone, naloxone, naldemedine, prucalopride and axelopran, which the Methods say were searched; no trial registries or grey literature.
Two investigators assessed articles independently with pre-designed forms (PDF p. 8).
All data extracted independently by two investigators (PDF p. 8).

domains.note: Cochrane tool by two reviewers covering sequence, concealment, blinding, incomplete data and selective reporting, but the table's yes/no entries have no key (several large phase 3 trials are 'No' for sequence generation without explanation).

domains.note: Random effects with heterogeneity explored; but an overall estimate pools eight drugs with I2 78%, an outlier was removed post hoc, and the side-effect table's ratios do not match its own counts (reporting issues).

Meta-regression and subgroups by opioid dose, laxative status, cancer pain, outcome definition and duration.
Funnel plot and Egger's test done and significant, but the asymmetry is put down to heterogeneity and its likely effect on the estimates is not discussed or carried into GRADE.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (no registered protocol, no list of excluded studies, publication bias found but not weighed), which by AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence in the review as a summary. This concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as an unbiased summary, not the trials themselves: they are randomized and placebo-controlled, the direction of effect is the same in almost all of them, and results hold in low-risk trials. The practical consequences are that the size of the benefit may be inflated by small-study effects, that the overall estimate mixes eight drugs, and that the side-effect ratios should be taken from the raw proportions.

key_findings.finding: Search to March 2017: 886 citations, 35 full texts, 26 publications with 28 placebo-controlled trials; one small methylnaltrexone trial removed as a clear outlier (all 11 on drug and none of 11 on placebo responded), leaving 27 trials: 23 of opioid-receptor blockers, 3 of lubiprostone and 1 of prucalopride; all published in English.

key_findings.finding: Funnel plot significantly asymmetric: Egger's test Z = -5.06, p < .001 with all trials, and Z = -4.79, p < .001 after removing the outlier; the authors attribute this partly to mixing drug classes and to heterogeneity (Q(26) = 105.0, p < .001; I2 = 77.9%).

FDA-approved drugs and doses only (lubiprostone, methylnaltrexone, naldemedine, naloxegol, naloxone): RR 0.69 (0.62-0.77), NNT 5 (4-7). reporting_issues.issue: Alvimopan: the text gives 433 of 1,060 people failing on drug (40.8%) (PDF p. 15) and Table 2 gives 1579 participants (PDF p. 31), but the forest plot (PDF p. 38) and Table 1 (PDF p. 27) give 1174 on drug and 519 on placebo (1693); the overall total of 5390 on drug matches 1174 (editors' sum of the forest plot).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 15, 27, 31, 38 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: The alvimopan failure rate on drug is about 37%, not 41%; Table 2's participant count for alvimopan is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall response on drug is printed as 2784 (51.3%) of 5390; 2784 of 5390 is 51.7% (PDF p. 12).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 12 of the accepted manuscript

reporting_issues.issue: Prucalopride: RR 0.88 (0.68-0.98) in the text and Table 2 (PDF pp. 17, 33) but 0.82 (0.68-0.98) in the forest plot (PDF p. 38); 0.82 fits both the interval and the counts (82 of 130 against 51 of 66 failing, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 17, 33, 38 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: The text value is likely a slip; the one-trial estimate is about 0.82.

reporting_issues.issue: In the forest plot, Webster 2017 (naldemedine) shows RR 0.81 (0.72-0.92), the same as the Chey 2014 (04) row, while its counts (65 of 177 against 37 of 61) give about 0.61 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 38 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: One trial's plotted estimate is probably wrong; the pooled naldemedine estimate may or may not be affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Methylnaltrexone: 1,619 participants in the text (PDF p. 14) against 1004 + 618 = 1622 in Table 2; pooled interval 0.49-0.78 in the text against 0.50-0.76 in the forest plot.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 14, 30, 38 of the accepted manuscript

reporting_issues.issue: The values in the adverse-event table's RR (log) column for diarrhoea (1.04), abdominal pain (1.07) and nausea and/or vomiting (1.03) do not match the printed proportions (8.5% against 4.7%, 12.8% against 5.5%, 11.5% against 10.1%; crude ratios 1.84, 2.32 and 1.14, editors' calculation); the abdominal-pain NNH interval (12.3-16.4) has its upper limit equal to the point estimate; the any-event NNH of 20.6 is given as 21 in the Results and 20 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 17, 18, 35 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: The relative risks of specific side effects cannot be used; the proportions can.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods define the NNH for an adverse event leading to withdrawal (PDF p. 10); the Results apply it to any adverse event (PDF p. 17).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 10, 17 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline NNH concerns any new adverse event, not stopping treatment; the NNH for stopping is 36.

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity for three lubiprostone trials is given as Q(1) = 1.40; three trials give 2 degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 16 of the accepted manuscript

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says study duration did not affect the RR of failure (PDF p. 4); the Results report trials of two weeks or less at 0.67 against 0.85 for the other 22, p < 0.001 (PDF p. 13), subgroup values that are also hard to reconcile with the overall 0.70.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 4, 13 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: Short trials may show larger effects; the duration analysis may have used a different model.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists alvimopan among approved treatments for OIC (PDF p. 4), but the analysis of FDA-approved drugs leaves it out (PDF p. 12).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 4, 12 of the accepted manuscript

reporting_issues.issue: The printed search strategies (PDF p. 39) do not include methylnaltrexone, naloxone, naldemedine, prucalopride or axelopran, which the Methods say were searched (PDF p. 7); the PRISMA checklist's search item reads 'Appendix S1 (need to include)' (PDF p. 42).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 7, 39, 42 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The GRADE explanation for naldemedine cites references 42-44, which are laxative reviews and a guideline, instead of the naldemedine trials (references 33-35).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 32 of the accepted manuscript

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says all studies showed superiority over placebo (PDF p. 18); four trials in the forest plot have intervals that include no effect (PDF p. 38).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 18, 38 of the accepted manuscript
reporting_issues.consequence: The consistency of benefit is overstated; the direction is consistent, the size is not.
